title: What is Engineering?
subtitle: Riley's Mindsets — Engineering Culture & Social Justice

people.name: Donna Riley
people.desc: Engineering professor at Smith College; author of Engineering and Social Justice (2008); argues engineers must confront structural inequities, not just solve technical problems.

terms.def: The set of attitudes and assumptions engineers hold about their work — problem-solving focus, pragmatism, and (Riley argues) uncritical acceptance of authority
Riley's goal for engineering: orienting practice toward equity and challenging structures that cause harm, not just solving assigned problems
The positive pragmatic trait Riley identifies: engineers' results-oriented drive to make things work despite obstacles
Riley's primary criticism: engineers solve problems as given without asking who benefits, who is harmed, or whether the problem should be solved

learn.title: 1 — Who is Donna Riley and What is Her Argument?
learn.body:
Donna Riley is an engineering professor whose 2008 book Engineering and Social Justice argues engineers should reorient their profession toward social justice rather than merely maintaining the status quo. The assigned chapter, "Mindsets in Engineering", examines the attitudes engineers hold about themselves — and that society holds about engineers.

Riley's core claim: mainstream engineering culture is dominated by a problem-solving mindset that focuses narrowly on technical solutions without asking whether solving the problem will actually improve the human condition — the phrase in Georgia Tech's own mission statement. She finds more negative than positive features in contemporary engineering culture.

learn.title: 2 — Positive Aspects of the Engineering Mindset
learn.body:
Riley does acknowledge positives. Engineers tend to be pragmatic and results-oriented — they care about making things work rather than debating endlessly. This "can-do" attitude enables large projects to get built and problems to get solved. Engineers also bring quantitative rigor and systematic thinking to complex challenges.

The emphasis on hands-on, applied knowledge means engineers understand real-world constraints that purely theoretical thinkers overlook. Riley sees value in these traits even as she critiques how they are deployed in practice.

learn.title: 3 — Negative Aspects: Conformity & the Status Quo
learn.body:
Riley's central critique is uncritical problem-solving: engineers are trained to solve the problem they are given, not to question whether the problem is worth solving or who benefits. This makes engineers "unlikely to question authority" — they execute decisions from managers, corporations, or governments without ethical scrutiny.

Engineering culture also tends toward political conservatism and resistance to social change. Perhaps most importantly, the profession's narrow technical focus means engineers rarely ask: who benefits and who is harmed? This ethical blindspot has contributed to disasters and injustices throughout engineering history.

learn.title: 4 — Engineering Jokes as Cultural Evidence
learn.body:
Riley uses engineering jokes as cultural data — a way to surface unconscious assumptions the profession holds. The jokes typically portray engineers as socially awkward, hyper-rational, and oblivious to human emotion. They also tend to be exclusionary, implicitly casting engineers as white and male.

The jokes reveal the self-image of the profession. If engineers laugh at portrayals of themselves as divorced from human concerns, those traits are being normalized rather than critiqued. Riley invites students to ask: do these jokes reflect your experience? Are they harmless fun or do they reinforce harmful stereotypes?

learn.title: 5 — Social Justice and the Engineer's Role
learn.body:
Riley's broader project is to reconnect engineering with social justice — the idea that engineers have a responsibility to consider the social, political, and environmental impacts of their work. GT's mission calls for improving the human condition, yet Riley argues this aspiration is systematically neglected.

A more just engineering practice would involve community participation in defining problems, awareness of whose interests technical choices serve, and willingness to challenge institutional power. This sets the stage for the course's broader examination of engineering as a historically and socially embedded practice.

reading.title: Engineering and Social Justice — Chapter 2: Mindsets in Engineering
reading.source: Riley, D. (2008). Engineering and Social Justice. Morgan & Claypool Publishers. Chapter 2, pp. 33–45.

paragraphs.text: This chapter uses engineering humor to draw out some mindsets commonly found in engineering and relates them to the intersection of engineering and social justice. Some mindsets are so much a part of mainstream engineering culture (or mainstream culture) that we may be unaware of alternative perspectives. The intent of this chapter is to separate the worldviews from the profession of engineering itself.

Engineering may be somewhat easier to define than social justice, but it too has a contested and changing definition. The earliest uses of the word engineer in the English language (fourteenth century) described 'a constructor of military engines' or 'one who designs and constructs military works for attack or defense.' In the nineteenth and most of the twentieth century, engineering was 'the art of directing the great sources of Power in Nature for the use and convenience of man.' As the field sought to move away from its identity as a trade into that of a profession, it emphasized its theoretical underpinnings in science and became thought of as the application of math and science toward useful ends — typically commercial, industrial, or military.

Before examining the relationship between engineering and social justice, Riley distinguishes the profession of engineering from some common mindsets found within the profession, particularly those mindsets that often stand in the way of engineering's intersection with social justice. While the profession currently and historically reinforces and helps create those mindsets, Riley believes it is only through recognizing the underlying mindsets and changing them that the profession can truly be transformed. The profession has a central role to play in bringing about this change.

Engineers and the engineering profession have some characteristics that prepare them well to work on social justice issues: the strong desire to be helpful and the persistence of a strong work ethic. Some engineering deans call for a public relations and recruitment campaign that presents engineering as a profession that serves humanity — citing examples such as bringing clean water and sanitation to a community, developing new drugs, designing renewable energy solutions to address climate change, or connecting people with wireless networks. Engineers are known for their work ethic; they are committed to getting the job done and will work long hours to make it happen.

There is something in the spirit of the engineer that wants to help. There is also a certain amount of overlap between the kinds of problems engineers solve and social justice problems, although the engineering approach may not define the problem to be solved in terms of social justice. The can-do attitude and work ethic that characterize engineering can be powerful forces for positive change when directed toward genuine human needs.

There are some structural problems with the profession — its military and corporate focus and the narrowness of engineering education, which excludes a number of important skills — that can present obstacles when engineers engage in social justice work. In addition, there is an engineering outlook that privileges scientific knowledge over other kinds of knowledge, prefers certainty to uncertainty, and seeks single, simplistic explanations for complex social phenomena.

Alice Pawley analyzes the narratives of engineering faculty members with an eye to the establishment and reinforcement of gendered boundaries in engineering. She uses three tools: space, time, and actors. Pawley establishes that engineers work overwhelmingly in private profit-oriented organizations and on industrial, commercial, and military problems. The centrality of managerialism in engineering may not be surprising, given that engineers are embedded in corporate organizations. Managerialism takes a systems approach to organizational management, viewing human relationships within the organization through a lens of inputs and outputs, increasing organizational efficiencies by minimizing inputs and maximizing outputs.

Engineering's embedding in military and corporate applications can explain the narrow sense of career path many students experience. Bruce Seely has documented the reform efforts in engineering education over the last century; one of the things they have in common is the recurring debate about how broad or narrowly focused an engineering degree should be and how much content from the liberal arts is appropriate. Generally, engineering students learn to think analytically only in certain ways appropriate to technical analysis: break problems down into small parts, solve the individual parts, and work back up to a solution. They typically do not come away with the ability to think critically, to question what is given, or question the validity of their assumptions. We do not learn, with any depth, critical approaches from the humanities and social sciences, and we do not learn many communication skills beyond writing technical reports and giving PowerPoint presentations.

Every profession has a series of jokes about itself, generally told within the group and drawing on some stereotypes about the profession. Clearly, not all engineers fit the stereotype, and some stereotypes are largely false. However, the jokes make some important contrasts between engineering and other professions, which reveal something about common mindsets in engineering which are less prevalent in other professions. If we look at these with an eye to cultural analysis, we can draw out some characteristics of these mindsets that are relevant to the intersection of engineering and social justice.

Joke 1 — The guillotine: A lawyer, a priest, and an engineer are scheduled to be executed by guillotine. The lawyer goes first, the executioner pulls the cord, but nothing happens. 'Double Jeopardy! You have to let me go!' And the executioner does. The priest is next — same thing. 'Divine Intervention! You have to let me go!' The engineer is next. As the executioner gets ready to pull the cord, the engineer cries, 'Wait! I think I see your problem...' This joke reveals a valuing of problem-solving abilities to a fault, an exclusive technical focus, and a willingness to accept authority — an unthinking loyalty even when it is the engineer's own neck on the line.

Joke 8 — The glass: To the optimist, the glass is half-full. To the pessimist, the glass is half-empty. To the engineer, the glass is twice as big as it needs to be. This joke is overtly about engineers' worldview — it reveals a mindset that will not evaluate a situation and refuses to make a subjective judgment. Is this a sign of uncompromising objectivity, or just bad design? Riley notes that these jokes are part of an oral tradition and are rich with cultural analysis; there is a combination of self-deprecation and celebration of these characteristics, an acknowledgement that many possess these mindsets and a recognition that they may not always produce desirable outcomes.

A positivist mindset often relates to two other perspectives commonly held in engineering: reductionism and technological determinism. Reductionism is the notion that phenomena can be broken down into smaller components for analysis and that analysis of the components can fully explain the system as a whole. Technological determinism holds that technology develops on its own in a self-propelling fashion — without regard to social forces — and that its innovations, in turn, impact society and drive political, cultural, and economic developments. This perspective is found in engineering when concern is placed on the impacts of technology on society without consideration for how society also constructs technology. Positivism and technological determinism lead many engineers to believe that their work is objective and that science itself is objective.

The conclusion: Engineers and the engineering profession have some characteristics that prepare them well to work on social justice issues — the strong desire to be helpful and a strong work ethic. Yet structural problems — military and corporate focus, narrow education — can present obstacles. In addition, there is an engineering outlook that privileges scientific knowledge, prefers certainty, and seeks simplistic explanations for complex social phenomena, creating political tendencies that eschew social justice and present real roadblocks in acquiring non-engineering skills needed for that work. In the next chapter, Riley begins to step outside the common mindsets in engineering by considering some critiques of engineering from a social justice perspective.

anki.q: What is Riley's central argument in Engineering and Social Justice?
anki.a: Engineers should orient their profession toward social justice rather than maintaining the status quo. The narrow problem-solving mindset neglects who benefits and who is harmed.

anki.q: What does Riley mean by the 'problem-solving mindset'?
anki.a: Engineers are trained to solve assigned problems efficiently without questioning whether the problem is worth solving or who benefits — a narrow technical focus that excludes ethical reflection.

anki.q: What positive traits does Riley identify in the engineering mindset?
anki.a: Pragmatism, a 'can-do' attitude, results-orientation, quantitative rigor, and hands-on applied knowledge.

anki.q: What is Riley's main criticism of engineering culture regarding authority?
anki.a: Engineers are 'unlikely to question authority' — they execute decisions made by managers and institutions without ethical scrutiny.

anki.q: How does Riley use engineering jokes as evidence?
anki.a: As cultural data revealing the profession's self-image — normalizing social awkwardness, hyper-rationality, and exclusion of women and minorities.

anki.q: What phrase from Georgia Tech's mission statement does Riley invoke?
anki.a: 'Improve the human condition' — Riley argues this aspiration is routinely ignored by mainstream engineering culture.

anki.q: What does Riley propose as a more just engineering practice?
anki.a: Community participation in defining problems, awareness of whose interests are served, and willingness to challenge institutional power.

anki.q: Why does Riley find more negative than positive aspects in engineering culture?
anki.a: The profession's emphasis on technical problem-solving suppresses ethical and political reflection, reinforcing existing social hierarchies.

anki.q: What connection does Riley draw between engineering and social conservatism?
anki.a: Engineering culture tends toward political conservatism and resistance to social change, making it less likely to challenge unjust structures.

anki.q: What is the Week 1 in-class assignment and when is it due?
anki.a: A short in-class reflection piece on the Riley reading, due Thursday August 27.

anki.q: What are the three sections of HTS 1081?
anki.a: Section 1: What Engineers Do; Section 2: Engineering in the 19th and 20th Centuries; Section 3: Ethics of Engineering.

anki.q: What are the three major exam events in HTS 1081?
anki.a: Two in-class essay exams (end of weeks 5 and 10) and a blue-book final exam (December 15, covering weeks 11–15).

anki.q: What percentage of the HTS 1081 grade comes from weekly assignments and quizzes?

anki.a: Solving the problem as given without asking whether it should be solved, who benefits, or who is harmed — Riley's primary critique of the engineering mindset.

anki.q: What makes engineering jokes culturally significant to Riley?
anki.a: They reveal the profession's normalized self-image: if engineers laugh at being socially oblivious, those traits are accepted rather than questioned.

anki.q: What is the 'can-do attitude' and why does Riley consider it both positive and problematic?
anki.a: Positive: it gets things built and problems solved. Problematic: it can mean charging ahead without asking whether the problem should be solved at all.

quiz.q: What is Donna Riley's central argument in Engineering and Social Justice?
options: Engineers should focus on social justice rather than the status quo
Technical expertise should override social concerns
quiz.explanation: Riley argues that engineers must move beyond narrow technical problem-solving and take responsibility for social justice.

quiz.q: What does Riley identify as a KEY NEGATIVE aspect of the engineering mindset?
options: Too much focus on social problems
Uncritical acceptance of authority and failure to ask who benefits
quiz.explanation: Riley criticizes engineers for being 'unlikely to question authority' — executing decisions without ethical reflection.

quiz.q: How does Riley use engineering jokes in her chapter?
options: As cultural data revealing the profession's self-image and exclusions
As proof that engineers lack humor
As a historical timeline of the profession
quiz.explanation: The jokes function as evidence of the values engineering culture normalizes — social awkwardness, hyper-rationality, and demographic exclusion.

quiz.q: What phrase from Georgia Tech's mission does Riley invoke to critique engineering culture?
quiz.explanation: Riley argues that GT's own mission calls for improving the human condition, yet engineering culture systematically neglects this aspiration.

quiz.q: What percentage of the HTS 1081 grade depends on in-class quizzes, discussions, and assignments?
quiz.explanation: Weekly quizzes, discussions, and other in-class work account for 50% of the grade, making attendance and participation critical.
